name: Diego Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, Diego. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Look, I buy car parts, brake pads, filters, batteries, wiper blades, for Calder Parts, a wholesaler that supplies about 400 independent garages around Millbrook. I start at seven, go through the overnight stock list on the big screen, then ring my regular reps at the manufacturers. Twenty years of that and I know which rep will find you 50 extra batteries in a cold snap. What wears me out is the new system. It tells me what to order and I spend half the morning checking whether it's right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say I told you so, the system's a glorified calculator. To my mates at the five-a-side I'd say the same and buy the next round. Online, I'm not on there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, it'd feel like winning an argument. I never took to these tools, and I'm not going to start now. If it's all hot air I keep doing what I do, and my 20 years of rep relationships still count for something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as now. I'd keep ringing my reps, keep checking the system's order suggestions by hand, and keep the mortgage overpayments of 300 a month going. Maybe I'd take a day to look at the system's reports, but only if the boss made me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. A bit relieved, actually. We've got the mortgage, and Mirela's job at the dental practice is steady, so there's no drama in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you check the system's orders by hand. How often is the system wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The system's order list is wrong about one time in twenty. Last month it wanted 300 oil filters for a model that's been discontinued. That's why my boss still needs me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of your life where you're already worried, before AI comes into it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The garages. Half of our customers are small, and the electric cars are cutting repairs. If the garages close, we lose customers, and that's a bigger worry than a computer.

say: I'd say the system is a **glorified calculator** and I told you so.
With my mates I'd say the same and buy the next round.
think: It would feel like **winning an argument**, since I never took to these tools.
My 20 years of rep relationships still count for something.
do: Carry on as now, ringing my **reps** and checking the system's orders by hand.
Keep overpaying the mortgage by **300 a month**.
feel: **Fine, even relieved**, with no drama because my wife's job is steady.
S0.quote: The system's order list is wrong about one time in twenty.
fieldNote: Diego's calm is **partial**: his real worry is the independent garages that buy from Calder, not AI.
He is proud of rep relationships and checks the system's output by hand.
Never uses AI tools by choice, so even a plateau leaves him exposed if the boss pushes them.

steps.text: Keep ringing the manufacturer reps every morning
Overpay the mortgage by 300 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say, show me. I've seen three systems come and go. To my mates I'd say it's coming for the office types first, and then I'd stop because I'm one of the office types.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this is where I'd get anxious. Buying, planning, checking are exactly what I do. Calder has six buyers, and I'm the one who still checks every order by hand, so I'm easy to point at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do what I hate: sit through the training, use the system in the mornings and learn what it does well. I'd take over the awkward suppliers myself, since the system can't talk someone round. And I'd put an extra 500 a month aside, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense. I'm not afraid of hard work, but I'm afraid of being the old man who wouldn't change. I'd hate to give my boss the satisfaction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd take the awkward suppliers. What would you say to your boss to make that your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, give me the ones where a human is needed: late deliveries, wrong parts, the guy who shouts. The system can't take a phone call from a shouting rep. And I'd show her last year's numbers, because that's the only argument she respects.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the team would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Greta, who's three years in and does all the repeat orders. She's good, but she does just the kind of thing the system will do. I'd tell her to learn the stock-planning side now, because I can't protect her.

say: I'd say **show me**, because I've seen three systems come and go.
With my mates I'd say it's coming for the office types first, then stop, because I am one.
think: Buying, planning and checking are exactly my job, so I'm **anxious**.
I'm the one who checks every order by hand, so I'm easy to **point at**.
do: Sit through the **training** and use the system each morning to learn it.
Take over the **awkward suppliers** myself, the ones needing a human.
Put aside an extra **500 a month**.
feel: **Tense**, mostly because I'd hate to be the old man who wouldn't change.
S1.quote: I'm not afraid of hard work, but I'm afraid of being the old man who wouldn't change.
fieldNote: Diego's resistance is **pride**, and he sees himself as easy to point at in the team.
His plan is to keep the human-only work: shouting reps, late deliveries, wrong parts.
Worries about junior colleague Greta, and tells her to learn the stock-planning side.

steps.text: Sit through the company's AI system training
Take over the supplier calls that need a person
Put aside an extra 500 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say nothing for a week, then ask the boss straight what happens to my job. To my mates I'd say it sounds like science fiction, but if it's true, we're in trouble. I'd call my brother, who works in logistics, and ask what he's hearing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think my job's gone and I won't see it coming. Two years isn't long enough for a man who's never opened one of these tools to learn them. The mechanics and warehouse lads get three extra years, but I'm all desk and phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd go through every household cost with Mirela and cut about 800 a month. I'd stop the mortgage overpayments, and keep the cash instead. I'd ask my boss about a move into sales or key accounts, where relationships matter, and I'd get a training course booked quickly, even though I hate that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, to be honest. Not shouting scared, quiet scared, the kind where you check the bank balance at night. We have about nine months of cushion, which is more than most, but it's not infinite.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the lads in the warehouse have three more years. Does that change how you see them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does. I'd be a bit jealous, which isn't fair, because they'd lose their work too. If I could, I'd back a plan where the company keeps us on for a transition year at full pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your son Luka that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my son Luka the truth, that I might lose my job and we'll be careful with money. He's fourteen and sharp, he'd notice anyway. I'd say it's not his fault and not mine, and we'll work it out.

say: At work I'd say nothing for a week, then ask the boss straight about my **job**.
With my mates I'd say it sounds like science fiction, but if true we're in trouble.
think: My job's **gone**, and I won't see it coming.
Two years is too short for a man who's never used these tools.
do: Cut about **800 a month** from the household budget and stop the overpayments.
Ask my boss about a move into **sales or key accounts**.
Book a **training course** quickly, even though I hate that.
feel: **Quietly scared**, checking the bank balance at night.
S2.quote: I'd tell my son Luka the truth, that I might lose my job and we'll be careful with money.
fieldNote: Diego's fear is **quiet**: he checks the balance at night and expects the job to go.
Envies the warehouse crew's extra three years, then admits that's not fair.
Honest with his son rather than hiding it, which fits his plain-spoken style.

steps.text: Cut about 800 a month from the household budget
Ask the boss about a move to sales or key accounts
Book a short AI training course right away
Ask the company for a transition year at full pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say five years is time to plan, and I'd ask the boss what the plan is for buyers. To my mates I'd say nobody knows, so keep your head down and do the job. I'd go to the garage owners I know and ask how they'd feel about us using AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel a bit of a reprieve. With five years I'd be 48 and Luka would be at university age, and I could get the mortgage down by about 30,000. But I'd still be a man who hasn't tried the new tools, which is the real danger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd start using the system properly, an hour a day, and see how it goes. I'd take a short course on key-account management, and I'd keep overpaying the mortgage. And I'd talk to the boss twice a year, in plain terms, about where I fit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd be able to hold it. It's like waiting for a storm you can see on the horizon. You can board up the windows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd start using the system properly. What would make that stick, given you've avoided it so far?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A date and a number. If I know that by the end of March I have to be able to run a full week of orders with it, I'll do it. I can't stand vague plans, but give me a deadline and I'll hit it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time change compared with the 2028 picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the 2028 picture I'd just be reacting, but with five years I'd be doing something about it. It's the difference between being hit by a car and crossing the road carefully.

To my mates I'd say nobody knows, so keep your head down and do the job.
think: I'd feel a **reprieve**, with the mortgage down by about 30,000.

Take a short course in **key-account management**.

feel: **Anxious but holding it**, like a storm on the horizon where you can board up the windows.
S3.quote: In the 2028 picture I'd just be reacting, but with five years I'd be doing something about it.
fieldNote: A **deadline** is what moves Diego, who says he hates vague plans but hits a clear date.
Five years gives him a reprieve, and he plans to cut the mortgage by about 30,000.
Plans a short key-account course to move toward relationship-based work.

steps.text: Run a full week of orders on the system by March
Take a short course in key-account management
Keep overpaying the mortgage towards a 30,000 cut
Meet the boss twice a year about where I fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say ten years is a long time, and most of us will have moved on by then anyway. To my mates I'd say it's a problem for the youngsters. And I'd say it with my fingers crossed, because Luka and Ana are the youngsters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel safer for myself, because I'd be 53 and might be retiring early or close to it. It's my kids I'd worry about. They'd leave school into a world where computers do the thinking, and I'd have no idea what to tell them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, keep paying down the mortgage so it's clear in about 12 years, and slowly learn the tools, one thing at a time. I'd save a bit more for the kids' studies. And I'd talk to Mirela about whether we could manage on less if I step back at 55.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A decade is a decade. Things that sound big usually arrive smaller, though I'd not bet on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd have no idea what to tell your kids. What would you say to your son Luka now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my son Luka to learn a trade with some thinking in it, like being an electrician or a mechanic who can run the diagnostics. People will always want the car fixed. That's the bit I'm sure of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do anything differently at work in the first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company to pair me with a younger buyer, so I learn the tools and they learn the reps' habits. Fair trade, and it keeps me useful.

say: I'd say ten years is a long time and **most of us** will have moved on anyway.
With my mates I'd call it a problem for the youngsters, fingers crossed.
think: I'd feel safer for myself at 53, maybe near **early retirement**.
It's my kids who worry me, because I'd have no idea what to tell them.

Save a bit more for the kids' **studies**.

S4.quote: I'd tell my son Luka to learn a trade with some thinking in it, like being an electrician or a mechanic who can run the diagnostics.
fieldNote: With ten years Diego's worry shifts to his **children**, and he admits he has no good advice.
Considers stepping back at 55, which stays tied to Mirela's steady job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, no question. Two years leaves a man who hasn't learned the tools with nowhere to hide. What would help is a transition year at full pay, a real course I can attend in work hours, and a boss who is straight with me. Plain notice, plain training, no slogans.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people think resisting new things is stubbornness. For me it's that I've seen what happens when a system gets it wrong and nobody knows enough to catch it. I'm not against change, I'm against being told it's fine.

headlineQuote: I'm not against change, I'm against being told it's fine.
portrait: Diego is a **43-year-old buyer** of car parts for a Millbrook wholesaler, with a wife who works at a dental practice.
He's centre in outlook, plain-spoken, and proud of **20 years** of rep relationships.
He avoids AI tools today and expects to be the one the boss points at, so his mood climbs fast.
Money cushions him but doesn't calm him: he fears being **the old man** who wouldn't change.
He responds to deadlines and clear plans, not slogans, and he worries most about his children.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries him most, because two years leaves nowhere to hide.
whatWouldHelp: A **transition year** at full pay, a real course in work hours, and a boss who is straight.
